rounds.question: Which take on the dot glass letters do you like best?
rounds.found: Six takes on the look the game has now, each with one idea, plus today's look for comparison. Every video is the same ten seconds: RAT is traced and becomes a word, it is sent and reaches the tower, new keys fall in, four letters are picked and taken back. The play links open the game with RAT traced in that look. All of them draw as fast as today's look or a little faster (measured at 640x480 on a slowed-down processor). Ideas can be combined: say which ones you want together.

options.title: Dot glass (now)
options.note: The game as it is today, for comparison: flat dark keys, the line through the letters, the light wipe over a real word, letters breaking into dots when sent, keys scrambling as they land.

options.title: Deep glass
options.note: Richer glass. Every key sits in a recessed well (dark under its top lip, the lower lip catching the light), each letter throws a soft glow on the dots round it, and the pane gets a faint curved reflection, darker corners and a glint that slides across now and then. Plays exactly the same.

options.title: Warm-up
options.note: Keys power on as they arrive. A falling key rides dark; when it seats, its whole letter strikes on with a short stutter (dark, a white flash, dim, then settling to amber) instead of the scramble of dots. The start of a night and every refill look like the set warming up.

options.title: Word lock
options.note: A stronger real-word moment. When the letters become a word every key of it flashes together, a ring of light opens out from each, the keys get a thick pale-gold frame and breathe as one, and the rest of the glass dips so the word stands alone. Replaces the light wipe.

options.title: Clear path
options.note: The traced order without anything crossing a letter. Lit links run from the edge of one key to the edge of the next and end in an arrowhead, a bead runs along each link, and a lit stud marks the first key. Replaces the line through the middles and the ring.

options.title: Lift-off
options.note: A more satisfying send. The letters rise whole off the glass, bigger and brighter, while the fill drains away down the keys under them and an ember of each letter fades; then they come apart into dots from up there, with a few sparks, and stream to the tower. The send takes about a tenth of a second longer.

options.title: Side meter
options.note: Deeper, more orange amber, and the value moved out of the letter's dot field: a stack of four small lamp sockets in the right edge of each key, one lit per value step, so the letter stands alone and the value reads like a little level meter.

rounds.question: How should the title menu look under the radio?
rounds.found: Five ways, four of them with each option in its own container on dark floorboards (no bare black). Pictures for a computer and a phone; play links open the title with that look (left/right or up/down to choose, A to pick).

options.title: Bar and parchment (now)
options.note: What you didn't like, for comparison: the game's wood-and-brass bar across the bottom with one parchment holding the list.

options.title: Brass plates
options.note: Dark floorboards under the sideboard, each option on its own brass plate side by side. The chosen one is lit from behind with a red arrow; the other sits in shadow.

options.title: Station buttons
options.note: Each option is a big cream push button, like the preset keys on an old radio. The chosen one is pressed in and glows amber.

options.title: Dial windows
options.note: Each option is its own little lit display in a brass rim, lettered in the radio's dot-matrix lights. The chosen one burns bright; the other is dim.

options.title: Parchment tags
options.note: Each option is a parchment tag hanging from the radio's base on brass chains. The chosen one is lit and sways gently.

rounds.question: How should the Carrier Lamp's red key look?
rounds.found: Five ways to mark the red key (it doubles any word that uses it), all without the red outline. Each clip shows the key on its own, then picked into a word: every look keeps it red when picked. Play links open the game with the Carrier Lamp fitted.

options.title: Red letter
options.note: The key's letter is lit red instead of amber, with a soft red glow round it. Picked, it fills red.

options.title: Red backlight
options.note: The letter stays amber; the dots behind it glow a dim, breathing red, like a red bulb behind the panel.

options.title: Ember fill
options.note: A low red glow sits in the bottom of the key and gently rises and falls, like embers.

options.title: Pilot lamp
options.note: A small red pilot lamp in the key's corner, softly pulsing, and its value dots turn red. The quietest of the five.

options.title: Red scan
options.note: A red line keeps sweeping down the key, like a signal being picked up.

rounds.question: Which title screen should the game open on?
rounds.found: Six ways in. The bar is now away on the title screen and rises into place with a clunk when you start. Options 1-5 use a placeholder logo made from the game's own letters (the real one drops into the same spot later); 6 spells the title in the radio's keys. Watch the clips, or play each one: press A once to skip the entrance, again to start. You can mix pieces.

options.title: Tuning in
options.note: The room starts dark with static and the dial hunting. Scrambled letters flicker and lock into the logo left to right, it lands with a thump, then the six lamps come on one by one.

options.title: From the tower
options.note: Rings of red signal leave the tower's beacon and wash across the room. The logo forms out of wavy lines that settle into the letters, then it burns in.

options.title: Neon across the street
options.note: The logo is a neon sign on a dark board. The letters buzz on one at a time, stutter, and flood the room red; SIGNAL lights up in amber under it.

options.title: Fill the tube
options.note: The signal tube along the bar fills itself cell by cell. When it's full the room flashes and the logo drops in on a brass plate with a heavy clunk and a bounce.

options.title: Programme sheet
options.note: Parchment, like the old title box: a sheet slides up, the logo is stamped onto it, SIGNAL comes up in red ink and the two lines of how to play type out.

options.title: Radio close-up
options.note: Your sketch, with your painted glass. No bar, the radio big and centred (a clean 1.5x). Static in the glass, then each letter of your picture switches on in reading order with a stutter and a blip; once lit they breathe, and now and then one flickers out for a moment. The dial scrolls, the meter swings up, the lamps come on and a brass PRESS START plate appears.

rounds.question: Which look should the letter keys in the radio glass have?
rounds.found: Six looks for the play area, all in the same room with the same value dots and the same lit state for traced keys. Play any of them in the game (press Select/Tab in the game to flip between all six too). Pick one, or tell me what to mix.

options.title: Pixel keys
options.note: Chunky pixel letters on dark keys; traced keys light up amber with dark letters. Matches the room's pixels exactly.

options.title: Typewriter
options.note: Round cream caps in brass rings with typed ink letters; traced keys glow warm.

options.title: Glow tubes
options.note: Dark glass with a fine mesh and thin orange letters burning inside, like old display tubes.

options.title: Neon glass
options.note: No keys at all: glowing letters floating in the smoked glass, traced ones burn white.

options.title: Ivory tiles
options.note: Chunky ivory game tiles with engraved letters; traced tiles turn gold.

options.title: Brass keys
options.note: Polished brass plates with stamped letters; traced plates flare bright.

rounds.question: Which play-area direction should we build on?
rounds.found: Five whole treatments of the glass, not just letter styles: how keys rest, light up, link together, lock when the word is good, leave for the tower and land. All stay dark with smooth warm glow and keep the value dots. In every one the glass flares when a word leaves, catches a red glint when the beacon answers, and its rim pulses red on your last word. Watch the clip, then play it. Pick one, or tell me which pieces to combine.

options.title: Valve bank
options.note: Your glow tubes taken all the way. Every key is a little valve: the letter is a hot filament that flutters, flares when the key lands and fills its glass with haze when traced. A live wire with current running down it joins the letters, and a sent letter leaves its valve dark for a moment.

options.title: Signal scope
options.note: No keys at all: the glass is one instrument screen. Green letters on a fine grid; the trace is a live wave that wanders while you search, then stands clean and turns gold when the word locks. Rings close in on traced letters and falling letters leave an afterglow.

options.title: Stencil plates
options.note: Heavy dark iron plates with the letters cut through them, and the radio's valves burning behind. You read the letters by the light in the cuts. Sent plates leave holes you can see the valves through, until the next plates slam down and shut the light off. Value dots are small drilled holes.

options.title: Switchboard
options.note: Every key is a jewel lamp in a brass ring. Tracing plugs a braided cord from lamp to lamp (it swings, then settles) and the lamp lights up. When the word locks the cords pull tight and a chase runs down the lamps; when you send, the cords drop away.

options.title: Dot glass
options.note: The keys are small lamp boards, cousins of the dial. A traced board fills up from the bottom and its letter goes white. A sent word comes apart into its dots, which stream out to the tower. Boards scramble for a blink when they land.
